sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The phase 1/2 CheckMate-040 and the phase 3 CheckMate-9DW trials consistently demonstrated meaningful activity of nivolumab plus ipilimumab (Nivo/Ipi) in previously treated and treatment-naïve patients with advanced HCC. However, patients with ≥50% liver involvement, Vp4 portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT), or bile duct invasion were excluded from these trials. We aimed to assess the real-world efficacy and safety of Nivo/Ipi in this high-risk population.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This international, multicenter, retrospective study was conducted in patients with advanced HCC who received Nivo/Ipi at six hospitals in Korea, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Taiwan between 2016 and 2024. Patients with Child-Pugh B/C or ECOG >2 were excluded.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of the 206 patients assessed for eligibility, 145 were included in the final analysis: 44 classified as high risk (Vp4 PVTT, n = 10; ≥50% liver involvement, n = 34; bile duct invasion, n = 7) and 101 as non-high risk. Baseline characteristics were comparable, aside from differences in liver function and high-risk features. Nivo/Ipi was administered as third-line or later-line therapy in 76.6% of patients. The high-risk group exhibited a significantly lower objective response rate (ORR) (12.8% vs. 34.3%) and shorter median progression-free survival (PFS) (1.2 vs. 2.9 months) and overall survival (OS) (3.6 vs. 16.5 months). Among the high-risk features, ≥50% liver involvement was strongly associated with inferior ORR, PFS, and OS, whereas Vp4 PVTT and bile duct invasion alone were not significantly associated with outcomes. A higher intrahepatic tumor burden was also inversely associated with treatment response and survival. Adverse events were more frequent in high-risk patients, particularly hyperbilirubinemia (36.4% vs. 13.9%; grade ≥3: 11.4% vs. 1.0%). On multivariable analysis, ≥50% liver involvement and prior immune-checkpoint inhibitor exposure independently predicted shorter PFS and OS.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Extensive liver involvement emerged as the key predictor of poor prognosis, whereas Vp4 PVTT and bile duct invasion were not associated with significantly worse outcomes.
Keywords: Hepatocellular carcinoma, Immunotherapy, Nivolumab, Ipilimumab, High-risk features

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) accounts for 75–90% of primary liver cancers and continues to pose a substantial global health burden [1–3]. A subset of patients presents with high-risk prognostic features – including ≥50% liver involvement, Vp4 portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT), or bile duct invasion – that are associated with dismal outcomes and limited therapeutic efficacy. Due to concerns regarding treatment-related complications and poor clinical outcomes, these patients are frequently excluded from pivotal clinical trials, resulting in a significant gap in evidence-based guidance for this subgroup [4]. Macrovascular invasion, particularly PVTT, is observed in 10–40% of patients with HCC and serves as a strong predictor of poor outcomes [4–6]. Among these, Vp4 PVTT – defined as tumor involvement of the main portal vein trunk or contralateral branches – represents the most advanced and clinically challenging subtype (online suppl. Fig. S1; for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/000551631) [5, 7].

The IMbrave150 trial, which established atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (Ate/Bev) as the standard first-line therapy for advanced HCC, notably included patients with Vp4 PVTT and recently reported a relevant subgroup analysis. Although Ate/Bev demonstrated improved survival outcomes compared with sorafenib in patients with and without Vp4 PVTT, the overall survival (OS) of those with Vp4 PVTT remained substantially shorter, underscoring the limited efficacy of current systemic regimens and the persistent unmet needs in this subgroup [8].

The phase 1/2 CheckMate-040 trial [9], conducted in the post-sorafenib setting, demonstrated meaningful and durable antitumor activity with the nivolumab plus ipilimumab (Nivo/Ipi) combination in advanced HCC. Subsequently, the phase 3 CheckMate-9DW trial, conducted in previously untreated, treatment-naïve patients with unresectable HCC, showed that Nivo/Ipi significantly improved OS compared with lenvatinib or sorafenib. Although subgroup analyses suggested that this benefit extended to patients with macrovascular invasion compared with the control group, individuals with Vp4 PVTT were not included in the trial [10]. Unlike CheckMate-9DW, real-world clinical practice frequently includes patients who have received prior systemic therapy before Nivo/Ipi initiation. Consequently, evidence regarding the effectiveness of Nivo/Ipi remains limited for high-risk patients, particularly those excluded from pivotal clinical trials.

Therefore, in this study, we aimed to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and safety of Nivo/Ipi in a real-world cohort of patients with advanced HCC and ≥50% liver involvement. Additionally, other high-risk features, such as Vp4 PVTT and bile duct invasion, were exploratorily analyzed due to limited subgroup sample sizes.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: This international, multicenter, retrospective study was conducted in patients with advanced HCC who received Nivo/Ipi between August 2016 and September 2024 across six institutions in the Republic of Korea, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Taiwan. Participating centers included the CHA Bundang Medical Center, Haeundae Paik Hospital, Ulsan University Hospital (Republic of Korea), Queen Mary Hospital (Hong Kong), National Cancer Center Singapore, and Taipei Veterans General Hospital (Taiwan).

Eligible patients had advanced HCC confirmed histologically or by noninvasive criteria according to the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases guidelines for patients with cirrhosis. The additional inclusion criteria included Child-Pugh class A and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–2. All patients received at least one dose of Nivo/Ipi. Data were extracted from electronic medical records at each center.

sec.title: Treatment and Assessment
sec.p: All patients were treated with nivolumab (1 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (3 mg/kg) or nivolumab (3 mg/kg) plus ipilimumab (1 mg/kg) every 3 weeks (four doses), followed by nivolumab monotherapy (240 mg every 2 weeks). Dose interruptions or reductions were implemented at the discretion of the treating physicians. Treatment continued until disease progression or the occurrence of unacceptable toxicity.

High-risk disease was defined by the presence of any of the following features: ≥50% liver involvement, Vp4 PVTT, or bile duct invasion. Patients were subsequently classified as either “high risk” or “non-high risk.”

Tumor responses were evaluated every 6–9 weeks according to Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumor version 1.1. Responders were defined as patients who achieved complete response or partial response, whereas nonresponders referred to those with stable disease or progressive disease as the best overall response during Nivo/Ipi treatment.

Progression-free survival (PFS) was defined as the interval from Nivo/Ipi initiation to disease progression or death, whichever occurred first. Patients without documented progression or who were lost to follow-up were censored at the date of the last follow-up visit. Patients who discontinued Nivo/Ipi due to its toxicity were censored at the time of the last administered dose. OS was defined as the time from Nivo/Ipi initiation to death from any cause. Adverse events were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Categorical variables were analyzed using frequencies and percentages and compared using Fisher’s exact test or Pearson’s chi-squared test, as appropriate. Continuous variables were analyzed using medians (range or interquartile range [IQR]) and compared using the Mann-Whitney U test. PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method, and differences between groups were evaluated using the log-rank test. Hazard ratios were calculated using multivariate Cox proportional hazards models. A two-sided p value <0.05 was considered significant. Analyses were performed using R version 4.4.2.

sec.title: Baseline Characteristics
sec.p: During the study period, 206 patients with advanced HCC were treated with Nivo/Ipi. Patients with Child-Pugh B or C liver function (n = 55) or an ECOG performance status of >2 (n = 6) were excluded. Hence, a total of 145 patients were included in the final analysis (Fig. 1). Of these, 44 patients were classified as the high-risk group, and 101 were classified as the non-high-risk group. Baseline characteristics were comparable between the groups, except for liver function and high-risk defining features (Table 1). The median age was 60 years (range, 18–83), and 83.5% (121/145) of patients were men. Nivo/Ipi was administered as the third- or later-line systemic therapy in 76.6% (111/145) of patients. Approximately 70.3% (102/145) of patients received a nivolumab dose of 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg, whereas 39.3% (57/145) had prior immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) exposure. Among the high-risk group, 77.3% (34/44) had ≥50% liver involvement, 22.7% (10/44) had Vp4 PVTT, and 15.9% (7/44) had bile duct invasion.

sec.title: Overall Cohort and Risk Group Comparison
sec.p: Among the 138 patients evaluable for tumor response, the objective response rate (ORR) was 28.3% (39/138), with a median duration of response (DoR) of 15.7 months. The disease control rate was 44.2% (61/138) (Table 2). After a median follow-up of 35.8 months (95% confidence interval [CI]: 31.5–39.5), the median PFS and OS were 2.3 months (95% CI: 1.8–2.8) and 9.5 months (95% CI: 7.3–16.5), respectively (online suppl. Fig. S2).

sec.p: The non-high-risk group had a significantly higher ORR (34.3% vs. 12.8%) and disease control rate (52.5% vs. 23.1%). Notably, among responders, the high-risk group exhibited a numerically longer median DoR (24.8 vs. 15.4 months) despite the small number of responders (Table 2). The median PFS durations were 1.2 months (95% CI: 1.1–1.7) in the high-risk group and 2.9 months (95% CI: 2.3–7.3) in the non-high-risk group (p < 0.01). Similarly, the median OS durations were 3.6 months (95% CI: 1.9–5.9) and 16.5 months (95% CI: 9.3–23.2) in the high-risk and non-high-risk groups, respectively (p < 0.01) (Fig. 2a, b).

graphic.alt-text: This figure demonstrates survival outcomes according to risk groups and liver involvement (<50% vs. ≥50%). Median progression-free survival and overall survival were poorer in patients in the high-risk group or with liver involvement of ≥50%.

sec.p: Furthermore, exploratory analyses comparing the two Nivo/Ipi dosing regimens (nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg vs. nivolumab 3 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 1 mg/kg) showed no significant differences in ORR (online suppl. Table S1), PFS, or OS (online suppl. Fig. S3). Moreover, 36.6% of patients (53/145) remained on treatment beyond the 12-week induction window, with 13.6% (6/44) in the high-risk group and 46.5% (47/101) in the non-high-risk group. Early treatment discontinuation was exclusively due to disease progression or death. Among induction completers, no significant differences in ORR (online suppl. Table S2), PFS, or OS (online suppl. Fig. S4) were observed.

sec.title: Treatment Outcomes according to Individual High-Risk Features
sec.p: The ORR was significantly lower in patients with liver involvement ≥50% compared with those with <50% involvement (3.2% vs. 35.5%; p < 0.01) (Table 2). A clear inverse correlation was observed between intrahepatic tumor burden and ORR (ranging from 46.2% in patients without intrahepatic lesions to 3.2% in those with ≥50% involvement) (Table 3). The median PFS was shorter in patients with ≥50% liver involvement compared with those with <50% involvement (1.3 vs. 2.9 months; p < 0.01) (Fig. 2c) and was significantly stratified according to intrahepatic tumor extent (p < 0.01) (Fig. 3a). The median OS was similarly inferior (3.3 vs. 16.5 months; p < 0.01) (Fig. 2d) and exhibited consistent stratification by intrahepatic tumor extent (p < 0.01) (Fig. 3b).

sec.p: The presence of Vp4 PVTT did not significantly influence ORR (30.0% vs. 28.1%; p = 1.00) or median PFS (1.7 vs. 2.3 months; p = 0.75) (Table 2; online suppl. Fig. S5A). The median OS was numerically longer in patients with Vp4 PVTT compared with those without (26.3 vs. 9.5 months; p = 0.56) (online suppl. Fig. S5B).

Although the number of patients with bile duct invasion was small (n = 7), their ORR (40.0% vs. 27.8%, p = 0.62) (Table 2), median PFS (1.2 vs. 2.4 months; p = 0.52), and median OS (2.1 vs. 10.1 months, p = 0.05) were comparable to those without bile duct invasion (online suppl. Fig. S5C, D). Multivariable Cox analysis identified ≥50% liver involvement and prior ICI exposure and a Child-Pugh score of 6 (vs. 5) as independent prognostic factors for shorter PFS and OS. Moreover, female sex was independently associated with worse PFS, whereas an ECOG performance status score of 1–2 (vs. 0) was independently associated with worse OS (Table 4).

sec.title: Safety Profile
sec.p: The most common treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of any grade were hepatitis (33.8%), pruritus (20.7%), elevated bilirubin levels (20.7%), anemia (17.2%), rash (14.5%), fatigue (14.5%), thrombocytopenia (13.1%), and neutropenia (10.3%). Frequently observed grade ≥3 TRAEs included hepatitis (9.7%), elevated bilirubin levels (4.1%), neutropenia (2.8%), pneumonitis (2.8%), adrenal insufficiency (2.1%), and rash (2.1%).

The overall incidence of TRAEs was comparable between the high-risk and non-high-risk groups, although elevated bilirubin levels were more frequent in the high-risk group (any grade: 36.4% vs. 13.9%; p < 0.01; grade ≥ 3: 11.4% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.01) (Table 5). Among individual high-risk features, ≥50% liver involvement showed a clear association with elevated bilirubin levels (any grade: 38.2% vs. 15.3%; p < 0.01; grade ≥3: 11.8% vs. 1.8%; p = 0.03) (online suppl. Table S3). In contrast, patients with Vp4 PVTT or bile duct invasion exhibited numerically higher rates of elevated bilirubin levels, although these differences were not significant (online suppl. Tables S4 and S5). Although patients with Vp4 PVTT showed no significant differences in TRAEs, bile duct invasion was marginally associated with a higher incidence of thrombocytopenia (any grade: 42.9% vs. 11.6%; p = 0.05; grade ≥3: 11.6% vs. 0%; p = 0.05).

fn.p: Values are presented as n (%). aDefined as patients with ≥50% liver involvement, Vp4 PVTT, or bile duct invasion.

sec.p: Exploratory analyses showed an overall trend toward more frequent any-grade TRAEs in the nivolumab 1 mg/kg plus ipilimumab 3 mg/kg group. However, no significant differences in grade ≥3 adverse events were observed between the two dosing regimens, except for hepatitis (online suppl. Table S6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this international, multicenter, real-world study, the survival outcomes and safety profile of Nivo/Ipi therapy were evaluated in patients with advanced HCC exhibiting high-risk features – such as ≥50% liver involvement, Vp4 PVTT, and bile duct invasion – who were excluded from pivotal trials, including the CheckMate-9DW [10] and CheckMate-040 [9]. The results demonstrated that the presence of these high-risk features was associated with significantly poorer survival outcomes and lower ORR compared with those without high-risk features. However, despite the overall poorer outcomes, responders within the high-risk group exhibited a numerically longer DoR, suggesting that a subset of these patients may still derive clinically meaningful and durable benefit. This finding underscores the importance of better identifying which subgroups of high-risk patients are most likely to respond to Nivo/Ipi. Notably, ≥50% liver involvement and prior exposure to ICIs were identified as independent predictors of poor prognosis, whereas Vp4 PVTT alone did not significantly affect outcomes. Additionally, TRAEs were more frequent and severe in the high-risk group, particularly in relation to liver function.

In this study, ≥50% liver involvement emerged as the strongest predictor of poor survival outcomes among patients with advanced HCC treated with Nivo/Ipi. This feature accounted for the majority of patients classified as high risk and consistently demonstrated a significant association with inferior outcomes in both univariable and multivariable analyses, even after adjusting for potential confounding factors. Notably, when patients were stratified based on intrahepatic tumor burden (none, <25%, 25%–50%, and ≥50%), a clear trend of progressively worse prognosis with increasing tumor burden was observed. Thus, the extent of liver involvement functions as a continuous prognostic factor rather than a simple binary high-risk indicator. Consistently, similar findings have been observed in studies of Ate/Bev therapy in advanced HCC [11], reinforcing the concept that extensive intrahepatic tumor burden is a key determinant of survival, independent of the type of combination therapy. Moreover, these findings are in line with previous meta-analyses [12] demonstrating the unfavorable prognostic impact of tumor burden in HCC and support the relevance of intrahepatic tumor burden in systemic immunotherapy. Our findings suggest that initiating Nivo/Ipi treatment at a lower intrahepatic tumor burden may be associated with more favorable outcomes. This observation is supported by the Japanese subgroup analysis of the CheckMate-9DW trial, which included a higher proportion of relatively early-stage patients (40% BCLC 0/A/B vs. 26% in the overall population) and demonstrated a remarkably favorable OS that was not reached (95% CI: 16.9 months to not estimable), compared with 23.7 months (95% CI: 18.8–29.4 months) in the overall Nivo/Ipi cohort [10, 13].

Vp4 PVTT was another defining feature of the high-risk group. In our cohort, Vp4 PVTT alone did not demonstrate a statistically significant association with inferior ORR or survival outcomes compared with patients without Vp4 involvement. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the limited number of patients with Vp4 PVTT, which substantially limits the statistical power. Accordingly, these analyses should be considered descriptive and exploratory in nature rather than inferential. While our real-world cohort showed survival patterns regarding Vp4 PVTT that differ from pivotal clinical trials such as the IMbrave150 trial [8], direct comparisons between these populations should be made cautiously due to differences in baseline characteristics and treatment settings. Larger prospective studies are required to clarify the prognostic and predictive implications of Vp4 PVTT in patients receiving immunotherapy-based systemic treatment.

In addition to liver involvement, prior exposure to ICIs was identified as an independent predictor of poor prognosis in our multivariable analysis. This finding is consistent with a recently published international multicenter study [14] demonstrating significantly lower response rates and worse survival outcomes in ICI-exposed patients treated with Nivo/Ipi compared with ICI-naïve patients. Specifically, the ORR decreased from 42.6% in ICI-naïve patients to 20.0% in those with prior ICI exposure, which may reflect acquired resistance to ICI therapy. Notably, ICI-naïve patients, despite multiple prior therapies, achieved an ORR comparable to that observed in the first-line setting of the CheckMate-9DW trial [10]. From a biological perspective, prior ICI exposure may induce multiple resistance mechanisms, including disruption of antigen presentation, T-cell exhaustion, and upregulation of alternative inhibitory immune checkpoints, which may attenuate subsequent immunotherapy efficacy [15, 16]. In addition to acquired resistance, primary resistance to Ate/Bev has been associated with an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment characterized by increased infiltration of regulatory T-cells, particularly in infiltrative HCC phenotypes [17], which may further limit responsiveness to later-line immunotherapy. Nevertheless, a subset of ICI-experienced patients in previous real-world studies achieved durable clinical benefit from Nivo/Ipi [14], implying that dual checkpoint blockade may still function as a rescue therapy in selected populations. This underscores the importance of identifying predictive biomarkers to optimize patient selection for sequential immunotherapy.

TRAEs were more frequent and severe in patients with high-risk features, particularly in relation to liver function. In the present study, the incidence of hyperbilirubinemia was significantly higher in the high-risk group compared with the non-high-risk group (36.4% vs. 13.9%), with grade ≥3 hyperbilirubinemia observed in 11.4% of high-risk patients and 1.0% of non-high-risk patients. Hepatitis – defined by elevations in aspartate aminotransferase or alanine aminotransferase – was also more commonly reported in the high-risk group, although to a lesser extent. Among individual high-risk features, ≥50% liver involvement demonstrated the strongest association with hepatic adverse events, whereas Vp4 PVTT and bile duct invasion were only associated with numerical differences. These findings collectively suggest that patients with extensive liver involvement are at increased risk of hepatic adverse events during Nivo/Ipi therapy and that the hyperbilirubinemia observed in high-risk patients may reflect pre-existing hepatic impairment rather than an intrinsic toxicity of the therapy. Accordingly, careful monitoring of liver function and early intervention for liver-related toxicities are essential in this vulnerable population.

The survival outcomes observed in the non-high-risk group of our cohort were shorter than those reported in the CheckMate-9DW trial [10]. This is primarily due to the high-risk nature of our real-world cohort: more than 75% of patients had been heavily pretreated (≥2 prior lines), and approximately 40% had prior ICI exposure. Additionally, our population had worse baseline performance status, more advanced disease stages, and more impaired liver function than the CheckMate-9DW trial participants. These fundamental baseline differences explain the survival gap between our cohort and the pivotal clinical data. In this context, although our study provides valuable insights into clinical factors influencing the efficacy and safety of Nivo/Ipi in routine practice, the predominantly heavily pretreated nature of the cohort suggests that our findings should be interpreted cautiously and not directly extrapolated to treatment-naïve populations.

Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the retrospective nature of the study introduces the possibility of selection bias and unmeasured confounding factors. Although multivariable analyses were performed, residual confounding due to baseline imbalances cannot be excluded. Second, the sample sizes, particularly within the high-risk subgroups such as those with Vp4 PVTT and bile duct invasion, were relatively small. Therefore, these subgroup analyses are limited by small sample sizes and may lack statistical robustness. Accordingly, these data need to be regarded as exploratory rather than definitive. Third, analyses restricted to induction completers are subject to substantial selection bias and should be interpreted cautiously. Fourth, this study exclusively included Asian patients, in whom hepatitis B virus infection is the predominant etiology of HCC, thereby limiting ethnic and etiological diversity. This may limit the generalizability of our findings to Western populations. Finally, the heterogeneity in clinical practice and patient management across multiple international centers may have influenced treatment outcomes.

In conclusion, this multicenter study demonstrated that high-risk features – particularly ≥50% liver involvement – were associated with significantly worse survival outcomes in advanced HCC treated with Nivo/Ipi, whereas Vp4 PVTT alone did not appear to adversely affect treatment efficacy. High-risk patients experienced more frequent and severe hepatic adverse events, highlighting the need for vigilant monitoring. These results support careful patient selection and risk stratification when using Nivo/Ipi and highlight the need for further studies to validate the findings and identify predictive biomarkers.

sec.title: Statement of Ethics
sec.p: This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the Declaration of Helsinki. Owing to its retrospective design, the need for informed consent was waived, and the study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of all participating centers (CHA Bundang Medical Center, Approval No: 2024-07-063; Haeundae Paik Hospital, Approval No: 2024-09-026; Ulsan University Hospital, Approval No: 2024-10-005; Queen Mary Hospital, Approval No: UW 24-714; National Cancer Center Singapore, Singhealth Centralized, Approval No: 2018-3046; and Taipei Veterans General Hospital, TPEVGH Approval No: 2023-08-010CC). All data were anonymized prior to analysis.
